title: AQA GCSE Physics · Energy Resources and Dissipation

items.stem: A torch is left switched on until its battery is flat. What has happened to the energy that was in the chemical store of the battery?

options.text: It has been transferred to light and to thermal stores, so the total is unchanged.
It has slowly been used up, so there is less energy now than at the start.
The part of it that was wasted has been destroyed inside the torch.
It is stored in the bulb and is released again when the torch cools.

items.why: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it has been transferred usefully and dissipated, leaving the total the same.

items.stem: A ball bearing rolls along a bench and slowly comes to rest. The ball, the bench and the surrounding air are treated as a closed system. What is true of the total energy of this system?

options.text: It has fallen, because friction has let some of the energy leak out of it.
It has fallen, because energy was used up in slowing the ball down.
It is unchanged; the kinetic store has emptied into the thermal stores.
It has risen, because the friction has created extra thermal energy.

items.why: In a closed system there is no net change to the total energy; the energy has only moved between stores inside it.

items.stem: In every system change some of the energy is dissipated. What does dissipated mean?

options.text: The energy is stored in the surroundings and later returns to the system.
The energy is stored in less useful ways, usually in thermal stores.
The energy is shared out equally between all the stores in the system.
The energy is destroyed as it spreads out into the surroundings.

items.why: This is what the specification means by dissipation: energy ends up in stores that cannot do the intended job.

items.stem: A food mixer is running. Which energy transfer in the mixer is best described as ‘wasted’?

options.text: The transfer to the kinetic store of the rotating blades.
The transfer that is destroyed by friction in the bearings.
The transfer to the room that flows back into the mixer later.
The transfer to the thermal store of the warm motor.

items.why: Energy that warms the motor is dissipated: it is stored in a less useful way and cannot turn the blades.

items.stem: The bearings of a machine are oiled regularly. Why does this reduce the unwanted energy transfers?

options.text: The oil takes in the wasted energy and stores it so it can be used again.
There is less friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal stores.
The oil removes the friction entirely, so no energy is dissipated.
The oil makes the moving parts lighter and so easier to turn.

items.why: Lubrication lowers the friction between the moving surfaces, so a smaller share of the input is dissipated.

items.stem: Thick insulation is laid in the loft of a house. Which statement about the house is now correct?

options.text: No energy can leave through the loft now, so the house never cools.
The insulation gives out warmth of its own and heats the rooms up.
The building now cools down more slowly than it did before.
The energy is destroyed inside the insulating material.

items.why: The insulation lowers the rate of energy transfer through the loft, so the building cools more slowly.

items.stem: Two saucepan handles are the same size and shape, but one is made from a material with a higher thermal conductivity than the other. Which statement about that handle is correct?

options.text: It transfers energy by conduction at a higher rate than the other one.
It transfers energy more slowly, because it holds the energy inside itself.
It transfers energy at the same rate, as the handles match in size.
It must be thicker in order to conduct energy at that rate.

items.why: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it.

items.stem: Two houses are identical except that one has thicker outside walls, built from the same brick. On a cold night, compared with the other house, the house with the thicker walls will

options.text: cool down faster, because there is more brick that has to be warmed up.
cool at the same rate, because the brick has the same conductivity.
warm itself up, because the thick walls give energy to the rooms.
cool down more slowly than the house with thinner walls.

items.why: For the same material, a thicker wall gives a lower rate of energy transfer, so the building cools more slowly.

items.stem: An architect wants a new building to cool down as slowly as possible on a cold night. Which change should be made to its walls?

options.text: Build them from a material that has a higher thermal conductivity.
Make them thinner so that less brick has to be warmed up first.
Make them thicker and use a material of lower thermal conductivity.
Make them thinner and choose a brick that conducts more quickly.

items.why: Both factors act the same way: greater thickness and lower thermal conductivity each lower the rate of cooling.

items.stem: In required practical activity 2, identical beakers of hot water are wrapped in different materials and the water temperature is recorded for ten minutes. Which result identifies the best insulator?

options.text: The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the smallest amount.
The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the largest amount of all.
The beaker whose water was the hottest when the timing started.
The beaker whose water ended at the temperature of the room.

items.why: The best insulator gives the lowest rate of energy transfer, so its water stays hottest and drops least.

items.stem: A student investigates how the thickness of an insulating layer affects the cooling of hot water in a beaker. Which measurements should be taken?

options.text: The temperature of the water at the end of the run, and nothing else.
The temperature of the room, measured at the start and again at the end.
The thickness of the layer, and the water temperature at set times.
The mass of the insulation and the volume of the water used.

items.why: AT 1 and AT 5 are exercised here: the length is measured with a ruler and the temperature is recorded against time.

items.stem: The student repeats the cooling run three times for each material and calculates a mean temperature drop. Why is this done?

options.text: So that the water is given more time in which to cool down properly.
To reduce the effect of random error and give a more reliable result.
To make every material finish at the same final temperature.
So that the results appear more careful than one run would.

items.why: Repeat readings scatter because of random variation; a mean of several runs is more reliable and reveals anomalies.

items.stem: A small electric motor is supplied with 800 J of energy. Of this, 260 J is transferred usefully to a kinetic store. What is the efficiency of the motor?
items.why: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer) = 260 J / 800 J = 0.325.

items.stem: Which statement about the efficiency of a device is correct?

options.text: A very well made device can have an efficiency of more than 1.
The efficiency of a device can never be greater than 1.
Efficiency is measured in joules when energy values are used.
Efficiency gives the fraction of the input energy wasted.

items.why: The useful output energy transfer cannot exceed the total input energy transfer, so the ratio is at most 1.

items.stem: A motor has a total power input of 1200 W and a useful power output of 900 W. What is the efficiency of the motor?
items.why: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input) = 900 W / 1200 W = 0.75, a ratio with no unit.

items.stem: (HT) A gearbox wastes energy because of friction between its moving parts. Which change would increase the efficiency of the intended energy transfer?

options.text: Lubricate the moving parts to reduce the energy dissipated.
Supply more power to the gearbox, so that it does more work each second.
Remove the friction completely so the gearbox is 100% efficient.
Run the gearbox for less time, so that less energy is wasted overall.

items.why: Reducing an unwanted transfer leaves a larger share of the input as useful output, which raises the efficiency.

items.stem: A student is asked to list the main energy resources available for use on Earth. Which list is correct?

options.text: Nuclear fuel, the tides, geothermal energy and water waves
Bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity and mains electricity
Coal, oil, gas and electricity from the mains
The Sun, wind turbines, the tides and bio-fuel crops

items.why: All four appear in the specification's list of the main energy resources available for use on Earth.

items.stem: Where does the energy supplied by a geothermal resource come from?

options.text: From sunlight that has warmed the ground during the day
From the hot rock lying deep below the Earth's surface
From fossil fuels that are burning deep underground
From fuel steadily burning deep within the Earth

items.why: Geothermal energy is the energy of hot rock underground, which is why it is available at all hours and in any weather.

items.stem: Which statement is the specification's definition of a renewable energy resource?

options.text: One with a supply so large that it could never all be used up
One that gives off no carbon dioxide while it is being used
One that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used
One that costs nothing to use once it has been built

items.why: This is the definition word for word: replacement keeping pace with use.

items.stem: Nuclear fuel is classified as non-renewable. Which reason for that classification is correct?

options.text: Uranium is mined from rock, so it is a fossil fuel
Nuclear power stations release carbon dioxide as they run
The clouds from its cooling towers add carbon dioxide
The uranium used is not replenished as it is used

items.why: Applies the definition directly: the fuel in the ground is not being replaced as it is consumed.

items.stem: Why is bio-fuel classified as a renewable energy resource?

options.text: The crops it is made from can be grown again as the fuel is used
It gives off much less carbon dioxide than burning coal does
There is so much plant material that it could never run out
It is made from living things rather than from rock

items.why: The definition is met: the supply is replenished, by replanting, at the rate it is drawn on.

items.stem: New coal is still slowly forming underground today. Why is coal still classed as non-renewable?

options.text: It is not: coal is renewable because new coal is still forming
New coal is forming far more slowly than it is being used
Coal gives off carbon dioxide, and renewables are clean
Coal supplies will have run out within about ten years

items.why: Replenishment has to keep pace with use. Coal takes millions of years to form and is burned in minutes.

items.stem: The specification gives three uses of energy resources. Which set of three is correct?

options.text: Transport, electricity generation and lighting
Electricity generation, heating and cooking food
Transport, electricity generation and heating
Heating, lighting and cooking in the home

items.why: These are the three uses named in the specification.

items.stem: Which energy resource supplies most of the energy used for transport worldwide?

options.text: Electricity from wind farms
Bio-fuel grown from sugar cane
Coal burned in steam engines
Oil, as petrol and diesel

items.why: Transport runs overwhelmingly on oil products; other resources supply only small shares.

items.stem: Panels on the roof of a house use the Sun to warm the water in a hot water tank. Which use of an energy resource is this?

options.text: Heating, because the Sun's energy is warming the water directly
Electricity generation, because solar panels make electricity
Transport, because that is a common use of energy
Electricity generation, then heating from the mains

items.why: The resource is the Sun and the job being done is heating; no electricity is involved at any point.

items.stem: Which group of resources is used for all three of transport, electricity generation and heating?

options.text: Wind, which could drive vehicles, power stations and radiators
Fossil fuels, which are burned for all three of these jobs
The tides, which run at all hours and serve every use
Nuclear fuel, used in stations, cars and in boilers

items.why: Oil fuels transport, gas and coal generate electricity, and gas and oil heat buildings.

items.stem: Why is a wind farm a less reliable energy resource than a gas-fired power station?

options.text: It is not less reliable, because the wind never stops blowing
Each turbine gives out less energy than a gas power station
Its output falls when the wind drops, whatever the demand
Wind turbines break down far more often than gas plants

items.why: Reliability is about being available when energy is wanted, and wind output is set by the weather.

items.stem: Tidal energy is described as a reliable energy resource. Which statement explains why?

options.text: The tides are driven by winds that blow daily
Tidal stations give out more energy than any other
The sea is pushed along by winds that never stop
The tides rise and fall on a known cycle

items.why: The times of high and low water are set by the Moon and the Sun and can be predicted years ahead.

items.stem: Which environmental impact arises directly from burning fossil fuels in a power station?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide are released into the air
Radioactive waste is produced and has to be stored safely
The steam from the cooling towers poisons nearby land
Acid rain is formed by the carbon dioxide given off

items.why: Burning releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming, and sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.

items.stem: Which statement about the environmental impact of renewable energy resources is correct?

options.text: They cause no environmental damage of any kind at all
They have impacts too, such as land flooded behind a hydro dam
Bio-fuel is the one renewable that has no effect at all on land use
Their only impact is the carbon dioxide released in use

items.why: Renewable does not mean harmless: dams flood valleys, wind farms alter landscapes and habitats, fuel crops use land.

items.stem: The share of UK electricity generated from renewable resources has risen sharply since 2010. Which explanation of this trend is best?

options.text: The UK's coal, oil and gas have now all been used up
Renewables can now supply power at all times without any backup
Concern about carbon dioxide, and cheaper wind and solar
Fossil fuels have been replaced completely across all energy use

items.why: Environmental concern plus falling cost is what has driven the change, supported by government policy.

items.stem: Scientists identified the harm caused by burning fossil fuels many years ago, yet their use has continued. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: The evidence is still too uncertain for anyone to act on it
Scientists have not yet explained the harm to any government
No other energy resource could possibly replace the fossil fuels
Political, social, ethical and economic factors count too

items.why: Science can identify an environmental issue but does not always have the power to deal with it; cost, jobs, public opinion and government policy all bear on what is done.
